arXiv:2611.34862v1 [cs.CV] 25 Nov 2026

BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding

Tomas Hodan   Vineet Bhat   Martin Sundermeyer   Jonathan Tremblay   Yash Patel    Médéric Fourmy   Stephen Tyree   Junwen Huang   Varun Burde   Martin Cífka    Eric Brachmann   Vincent Lepetit   Stan Birchfield   Jiri Matas   Carsten Rother Affiliation: Mistral  NYU  Google  NVIDIA  CTU Prague  TU Munich  Niantic Spatial  ParisTech  Heidelberg Uni.Online evaluation system: https://bop.felk.cvut.cz/refer
Abstract

We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} in 2D but only 12.4% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object’s size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.

1 Introduction

3D object grounding, which is the task of 3D localization of objects referred to by a natural-language expression from visual or 3D input, is important for systems that act in the physical world [16, 1]. Robots need 3D information for grasping, AR systems for augmenting objects with virtual content, and navigation systems for reaching named targets. We focus on the monocular variant [99], predicting 3D bounding boxes from a single image with known intrinsics rather than from the reconstructed point cloud assumed by most 3D grounding methods. This variant needs only a calibrated camera, as found on phones, robots, and AR/VR headsets.

While 2D grounding has been studied extensively, with task-specific detectors [58, 68] and more recently general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) [80, 6, 36], the 3D counterpart remains underexplored. Three factors make it harder: (1) the expected output is an oriented 3D box rather than an axis-aligned rectangle, (2) ground truth is hard to obtain at scale, and (3) a single monocular view leaves object scale and distance jointly underdetermined. Existing 3D grounding benchmarks focus on room-scale indoor or traffic scenes [16, 1, 99, 48], open-vocabulary 3D detectors are evaluated with category-level queries rather than free-form referring expressions [93, 56, 71], and few evaluate 2D and 3D grounding together [23, 27], leaving it unclear whether errors arise in localizing the referred objects in the image or in estimating their 3D position, size, or orientation.

To address these limitations, we introduce BOP-Refer, a benchmark for 3D and 2D object grounding built on top of BOP (Benchmark Object Pose) [52, 75], an established benchmark suite for 6DoF object pose estimation that includes a wide range of datasets with accurate 3D object models and pose annotations. Our key contributions are:

  1. 1.

    First benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of diverse objects from referring expressions. BOP-Refer covers 225 diverse everyday and industrial objects from 9 BOP datasets, with 1,400 validation and 1,400 test image-query pairs. We provide VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions (Fig. BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding) with high-quality ground-truth 3D and 2D boxes, for direct comparison of 3D and 2D grounding on the same data.

  2. 2.

    Comprehensive evaluation of frontier VLMs. We evaluate 12 proprietary and 5 open-weight VLMs from the Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families, revealing that monocular 3D grounding remains far from solved, whereas the strongest models already localize most referred objects well in 2D. Our analysis points to metric scale estimation (the distance and size of the objects) as the main source of error in 3D grounding.

  3. 3.

    Symmetry-aware 3D evaluation. We introduce two symmetry-aware 3D box comparison functions that treat symmetry-related 3D boxes as equivalent: a variant of the popular IoU3D, and NCD (Normalized Corner Distance), which can distinguish near and far misses.

  4. 4.

    Online evaluation system. We developed an online evaluation system that scores submissions on the test split with private ground-truth annotations and provides a public leaderboard of submitted methods. The validation split has public ground truth for development.

2 Related work

2.1 2D grounding

Classical 2D grounding benchmarks such as RefCOCO [60], RefCOCO+ [96], and RefCOCOg [72], derived from MSCOCO [66], pair each expression with a single region, whereas Flickr30k Entities [82] and gRefCOCO [67, 30] also include multi-target expressions, as BOP-Refer does. Chen et al. [17] report labeling error rates of up to 24% in the RefCOCO family; BOP-Refer minimizes such errors by deriving ground truth from 3D object models in annotated 6DoF poses and by verifying every query by hand. Open-vocabulary detectors such as MDETR [58], GLIP [62], Grounding DINO [68], and OWLv2 [74], and general-purpose VLMs such as Kosmos-2 [80], the Qwen-VL series [6, 7], Gemini [36], and Molmo [28] predict 2D boxes or points from referring expressions. The strongest reach ∼\sim90% accuracy on RefCOCO, where scores are saturating [17], motivating our harder monocular 3D setting.

2.2 3D grounding

ScanRefer [16], ReferIt3D [1], and the multi-target Multi3DRefer [102] ground expressions in reconstructed ScanNet [26] point clouds. The monocular setting is addressed by Mono3DRefer [99], built on KITTI [32] with LLM-generated, human-verified queries, and by MM3DRefer and MT3DRefer [48], which add multiple objects and the Rope3D [94] dataset (see also MonoMulti3D-ROPE [47]). All match BOP-Refer’s setting: predicting a 3D box from a single image with known intrinsics and a referring expression. Of these, only Mono3DRefer is publicly available, making it BOP-Refer’s closest released counterpart (Tab. 1). BOP-Refer differs by covering everyday and industrial objects rather than driving scenes, unifying 2D and 3D evaluation, and deriving amodal ground truth from 3D object models in 6DoF poses rather than from LiDAR.

Specialist models such as OVMono3D [93], DetAny3D [100], and WildDet3D [56] detect objects in 3D from category labels or 2D prompts, and LocateAnything3D [71], a VLM-based detector that also supports grounding, is evaluated only with templated category and location prompts (e.g., “chair on the left”) rather than free-form referring expressions, all on Omni3D [12], which has no per-object symmetry handling. Boxer [29], SAM 3D [19], and GR3D [21] lift 2D detections, masks, or grounded regions to 3D, and Oryon and Horyon [24, 25] estimate a text-described object’s pose from two RGB-D views. Other 3D work, such as the Ego-Exo4D [44] correspondence task, ExCap3D [95], Cubify Anything [61], and SpatialLM [73], does not ground free-form text to 3D boxes in a single image.

2.3 Spatial reasoning

Beyond the grounding benchmarks above, spatial reasoning in VLMs is evaluated through visual question answering with text answers, e.g., by SpatialVLM [15], 3DSRBench [70], 3D-LLM [54], and RoboSpatial [88], or through 2D pointing at objects and regions, e.g., by PointArena [22] (spatial, affordance, and counting queries). SpatialRGPT [20] and Q-Spatial Bench [64] ask about metric distances and sizes, and the latter shows that reference objects of known size help VLMs. BOP-ASK [9], also built on BOP datasets, provides 33M question-answer pairs for object-interaction reasoning, including referred-object poses. BOP-Refer instead targets text-to-box grounding with human-verified queries, 2D and 3D ground-truth boxes, and symmetry-aware metrics, which broad VLM benchmarks such as MMMU [97], MMBench [69], and MMStar [18] do not cover.

2.4 Vision-language models

Many recent VLMs output 2D bounding boxes or points: the Gemini family [35, 38], Gemini Robotics ER 2 [43, 37] (a Gemini variant tuned for embodied reasoning), Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7 [3, 4], Gemma 4 [34], and the Qwen-VL family [7] document 2D boxes, and GPT-5.4 and 5.5 [76, 77] return them when asked for pixel coordinates. A 3D box format is documented only for Gemini and for Qwen since Qwen3-VL, carried over to Qwen3.5 [84] and Qwen3.6 [85]. Their monocular 3D grounding remains largely untested: the few works that benchmark frontier closed VLMs on it cover one to three such models each, with category-level queries in room-scale scenes or referring expressions in driving scenes. Gemini Robotics [33] and the Seed1.5-VL [46] and Qwen3-VL [7] reports evaluate Gemini models on SUN-RGBD, MM-Spatial [27] evaluates GPT-4V and GPT-4o on indoor 3D grounding, and MonoVLM [83] and M3SunAgent [101] evaluate GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 on Mono3DRefer [99], where they trail specialized methods. Qwen3-VL is moreover trained on 3D data in Omni3D’s camera convention [12], so its Omni3D results are in-distribution.

3 BOP-Refer benchmark

This section defines the 3D and 2D grounding tasks and their metrics (Secs. 3.1 and 3.2), describes the source BOP datasets and the data splits (Sec. 3.3), and explains how the text queries are generated and human-verified (Sec. 3.4). Supp. Sec. F details how the ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes are derived from the BOP annotations.

3.1 3D object grounding

Input and output.

Given a monocular image II (RGB or monochrome) from a pinhole camera with known intrinsic matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K}, and a text query qq referring to potentially multiple visible objects, the goal is to estimate oriented 3D bounding boxes {b3​D,i}i=1N\{b_{\mathrm{3D},i}\}_{i=1}^{N} of the referred objects. Each 3D box is parameterized as b3​D,i=(𝐑,𝐭,𝐬)b_{\mathrm{3D},i}=(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{s}), where (𝐑,𝐭)∈S​E​(3)(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t})\in SE(3) is the rigid transformation from the box’s local frame BB (origin at the box center, axes aligned with the box edges) to the camera frame, and 𝐬∈ℝ+3\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{+} are the full extents along the three box axes. A point 𝐩B\mathbf{p}_{B} expressed in BB thus maps to the camera frame as 𝐑​𝐩B+𝐭\mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{p}_{B}+\mathbf{t}, and the 8 box corners are (±sx/2,±sy/2,±sz/2)(\pm s_{x}/2,\pm s_{y}/2,\pm s_{z}/2) in BB. The bounding boxes are amodal (covering the entire referred objects, including any occluded parts) and have axes aligned with the object’s symmetries, if any (see Supp. Sec. F for a precise definition).

Known intrinsics.

In practice, intrinsics are readily available in target deployment scenarios such as smartphones, robots, and AR/VR headsets. Geometrically, the focal length, object size, and distance are jointly unconstrained from a single view without intrinsics. Providing intrinsics resolves the focal length and leaves only the size-versus-distance ambiguity. The remaining problem is ill-posed but, we hypothesize, largely resolvable through learned priors about typical object sizes and scene layouts [98] that VLMs acquire from large-scale visual training data. Our error analysis shows that current VLMs do not yet resolve this ambiguity (Sec. 4.4).

Measuring accuracy.

On the 3D grounding task, we report two variants of Average Precision, APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, which differ in the underlying box comparison function (Fig. 2) and thresholds of correctness. APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} scores predicted 3D boxes with our symmetry-aware Normalized Corner Distance (NCD) defined below and applies thresholds δ∈{0.2,0.4,…,2.0}\delta\in\{0.2,0.4,\ldots,2.0\}, where δ=1\delta=1 corresponds to a mean corner error of one box diagonal. APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} is computed as in Omni3D [12] over thresholds τ∈{0.05,0.10,…,0.50}\tau\in\{0.05,0.10,\ldots,0.50\}11 1 IoU3D thresholds are lower than the IoU2D thresholds (Sec. 3.2) because monocular 3D prediction is hard (see Fig. 11 in [12]). but using our symmetry-aware variant of Intersection over Union (IoU3D), also defined below.22 2 A prediction is a true positive if NCD≤δ\text{NCD}\leq\delta for APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and if IoU3D≥τ\text{IoU3D}\geq\tau for APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, so a larger δ\delta is looser and a larger τ\tau stricter. We introduce NCD because IoU3D cannot distinguish a near from a complete miss (Fig. 2c): once the predicted and ground-truth boxes stop overlapping, IoU3D becomes zero, which is especially problematic for thin or small objects. To prevent BOP datasets with more samples from dominating APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, both metrics are computed per dataset and then averaged. Details on the evaluation methodology are in Supp. Sec. H.

Normalized Corner Distance (NCD).

We define NCD as the mean L2 distance between the 8 corresponding corners of the predicted box b^3​D\smash[t]{\hat{b}}_{\mathrm{3D}} and the ground-truth box b3​Db_{\mathrm{3D}}, normalized by the ground-truth box diagonal d⁡(b3​D)d(b_{\mathrm{3D}}), so that 1.01.0 means the corners are off by one diagonal on average:

NCD​(b^3​D,b3​D,𝒮)=min𝐒∈𝒮⁡minπ∈Π18​d​(b3​D)​∑i=18∥𝐜i​(b^3​D)−𝐜π⁡(i)​(𝐒∘b3​D)∥2,\text{NCD}(\hat{b}_{\mathrm{3D}},b_{\mathrm{3D}};\mathcal{S})=\min_{\mathbf{S}\in\mathcal{S}}\,\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\\ \frac{1}{8\,d(b_{\mathrm{3D}})}\sum_{i=1}^{8}\big\lVert\mathbf{c}_{i}(\hat{b}_{\mathrm{3D}})-\mathbf{c}_{\pi(i)}(\mathbf{S}\circ b_{\mathrm{3D}})\big\rVert_{2}, (1)

where 𝐜i​(⋅)\mathbf{c}_{i}(\cdot) is the ii-th corner of a box. We denote by 𝒮\mathcal{S} the set of symmetry transformations of the target object, given by the symmetry annotations of BOP [53] (available for all BOP objects, with continuous rotational symmetries discretized into a finite set) and including the identity. Applying any of them to the ground-truth box yields an equally valid box. The inner minimum resolves the ambiguity of corner labels. The same box can be described with its axes, and hence its corners, labeled in 24 different ways, and Π\Pi is the set of the 24 corresponding corner permutations (Supp. Sec. H.2). Without this minimum, a prediction that describes the ground-truth box with differently ordered axes would get a nonzero NCD. With it, NCD depends on the two boxes only as sets of points, and NCD=0\text{NCD}=0 if and only if the predicted box coincides with 𝐒∘b3​D\mathbf{S}\circ b_{\mathrm{3D}} for some 𝐒∈𝒮\mathbf{S}\in\mathcal{S}. IoU3D, introduced below, compares volumes, which do not depend on corner labels, so it maximizes over 𝒮\mathcal{S} only.

Intersection over Union (IoU3D).

For a predicted box b^3​D\smash[t]{\hat{b}}_{\mathrm{3D}} and a ground-truth box b3​Db_{\mathrm{3D}}, our symmetry-aware variant of IoU3D maximizes the ratio of their intersection volume to their union volume over the symmetry transformations 𝒮\mathcal{S}:

IoU3D​(b^3​D,b3​D,𝒮)=max𝐒∈𝒮⁡|b^3​D∩(𝐒∘b3​D)||b^3​D∪(𝐒∘b3​D)|,\text{IoU3D}(\hat{b}_{\mathrm{3D}},b_{\mathrm{3D}};\mathcal{S})=\max_{\mathbf{S}\in\mathcal{S}}\frac{\lvert\hat{b}_{\mathrm{3D}}\cap(\mathbf{S}\circ b_{\mathrm{3D}})\rvert}{\lvert\hat{b}_{\mathrm{3D}}\cup(\mathbf{S}\circ b_{\mathrm{3D}})\rvert}, (2)

where |⋅|\lvert\cdot\rvert denotes volume. We use this IoU3D variant as many BOP objects are symmetric and geometrically equivalent poses can therefore yield different box orientations. As a concrete example, consider an upright cylinder. Any box obtained by rotating a valid box about the cylinder axis is equally valid, yet two such boxes with square cross-sections differing by 45∘45^{\circ} have a volume ratio of only 0.710.71 before the maximization, whereas IoU3D=1\text{IoU3D}=1 correctly scores them as equivalent. Prior symmetry-aware variants of IoU3D [91, 2] consider only rotations about a single symmetry axis of rotationally symmetric object categories, whereas ours covers all discrete and continuous symmetries annotated for each object. In BOP-Refer, 78 of the 225 objects have at least one discrete or continuous symmetry.

3.2 2D object grounding

Input and output.

Given an image II and a text query qq referring to one or more visible objects, the goal is to estimate their amodal 2D bounding boxes {b2​D,i}i=1N\{b_{\mathrm{2D},i}\}_{i=1}^{N}. Unlike in 3D, no camera intrinsics are given, as 2D boxes do not depend on them. Amodal means each box is the tightest axis-aligned rectangle around the whole object, including occluded parts. Each 2D box is b2​D,i=(x1,y1,x2,y2)b_{\mathrm{2D},i}=(x_{1},y_{1},x_{2},y_{2}), its top-left and bottom-right corners in pixels.

Measuring accuracy.

We report the Average Precision (APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}) computed with the same matching, pooling, and per-dataset macro-averaging protocol as APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} (Sec. 3.1) but using IoU2D of axis-aligned boxes in place of IoU3D. Following COCO [66], we use IoU2D thresholds τ∈{0.50,0.55,…,0.95}\tau\in\{0.50,0.55,\ldots,0.95\} and compute APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} as the average over the thresholds (per-threshold values in Supp. Tab. 11).

3.3 Benchmark dataset

Source datasets.

BOP-Refer is built on 9 BOP datasets: six everyday-object datasets (HOT3D [8], HANDAL [45], HOPEv2 [89], LM [49], HB [59], YCB-V [92]) and three industrial-object datasets (T-LESS [51], ITODD [31], IPD [57]), which together contain 227 unique objects, 225 of which are referred to by the BOP-Refer queries. The datasets include accurate 3D object models and images of the objects in various scenes, annotated with 6DoF poses. We use the models and pose annotations to derive the ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes (Supp. Sec. F) and to generate the referring text queries (Sec. 3.4). Fig. BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding shows sample images and queries from each dataset, and Supp. Tab. 15 lists per-dataset image counts and modality.

Image modality.

Images are RGB, except in ITODD, IPD, and the Quest 3 subset of HOT3D, which are monochrome. Although some datasets include depth images, we use only 2D images to keep the input modality consistent. Fisheye images from HOT3D were undistorted to a pinhole model.

Dataset samples.

Each sample consists of an image, camera intrinsics, a free-form natural-language query, and ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects. A single query may refer to a single object (e.g., “the biggest mug”) or multiple objects (e.g., “all mugs on the table”). To support symmetry-aware evaluation, the ground-truth 3D bounding boxes are associated with discrete and continuous symmetry transformations of the objects.

Validation and test splits.

We provide validation and test splits, each containing 1,400 real images drawn from the 9 BOP datasets listed above, with one text query per image. Ground-truth annotations are publicly available for the validation split but held private for the test split (accessible only through the online evaluation system). We deliberately keep the splits compact to keep evaluation affordable even for large VLMs, and curate samples across datasets, query types, and target objects to ensure breadth. This matches popular grounding and VLM evaluation splits, which range from ∼900{\sim}900 to ∼3,000{\sim}3{,}000 samples (e.g., PointArena [22], BOP-ASK [9], MMMU [97], MMBench [69]).

No dedicated training split.

BOP-Refer is an evaluation-only benchmark and by design does not provide any training split, leaving the choice of training data to each evaluated approach. Training data can be generated by applying our query-generation pipeline (Sec. 3.4, code in the BOP-Refer toolkit) to any images with 3D object annotations, e.g., the BOP training images of the same objects.

3.4 Text query generation

Generation procedure.

Text queries are generated by two VLMs (GPT-5.4 [76] and Gemini 3.1 Pro [39]) to reduce model-specific bias. For each image, we first construct a scene graph that encodes object attributes and pairwise spatial relations. Object attributes include the normalized 2D bounding box, depth, visibility fraction, apparent- and physical-size ranks, and a human-readable position description. Pairwise relations cover direction, depth ordering, proximity, occlusion, support, and relative size, each qualified, where applicable, by a small, moderate, or large margin. We also pre-generate an appearance description of each object with the two VLMs, from 8 canonical views rendered from its 3D model. Each of the generator VLMs is then prompted with the image, the camera intrinsics, the scene graph in YAML form, and the object appearance descriptions, and is asked to select one or more target objects and produce 5 candidate referring expressions covering a mix of strategies (appearance, spatial-relational, comparative, functional, and multi-object). Note that the generators receive strictly more information than the models being evaluated, which receive only the image, the query, and (in the 3D task) the camera intrinsics. Details are in Supp. Sec. G.

Quality assurance.

Generated queries went through two filtering stages: (1) automatic verification, where Claude Opus 4.7 checked each query against 14 criteria, including unambiguity, and rejected it if any failed, and (2) human verification, where 25 recruited reviewers inspected the remaining queries in a dedicated tool and rewrote or discarded those still judged incorrect or ambiguous. Finally, one query per image was kept, balancing object coverage and including multi-target queries. Automatic verification keeps 49 to 71% of the 21,190 candidate test queries, depending on the source dataset, and the human reviewers accept at least one query for 81% of the inspected samples (Supp. Secs. G.2 and G.3).

4 Experiments

We evaluate a diverse set of state-of-the-art VLMs from the Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, and Gemma families, alongside four specialist 3D grounding pipelines (WildDet3D, Boxer, SAM 3D, and mask back-projection). No model is fine-tuned on the benchmark. We report test-split results here and validation-split results in Supp. Sec. C. Three key ablations are in Sec. 4.3, and further ones in Supp. Sec. A.

4.1 Evaluated methods

VLMs.

We evaluate 12 proprietary and 5 open-weight models. The proprietary ones are Gemini Robotics ER 2 [43], four more Gemini models (3.1 Pro [39], 3.8 Flash [40], 4 Argon [41], and 4 Carbon [42]), four GPT models (5.4 and 5.5 [76, 77], 6 Astra [79], and 6.1 Sol [78]), and three Claude models (Opus 4.6 [3], 4.7 [4], and 5.5 [5]), all of which output 2D boxes (Sec. 2.4). The open-weight ones are three successive Qwen releases with native 2D box prediction, Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B [7] and its natively multimodal successors Qwen3.5-397B-A17B [84] and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [85], as well as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [86], an open-weight preview of the architecture planned for Qwen4 (125B parameters, 6B active), and Gemma 4 31B [34]. Each model is evaluated 3 times on both tasks with the same inputs and settings in every run. We report the mean and standard deviation over these runs in all result tables.

VLM prompting strategy.

Each VLM receives the image, the text query, and a specification of the output format. In 2D, each family receives its documented prompt and box format where one exists; GPT, which documents none, receives a prompt similar to Claude’s. In 3D, all models receive the same prompt, our own: it asks for the 9-DoF box format published for Gemini and Qwen (center, size, and roll/pitch/yaw angles), provides the camera intrinsics, and includes 5 text-only in-context examples. Proprietary models run at medium reasoning effort, and Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6, and Qwen3.8 Flash Next with thinking on, except Qwen3.6 in 3D, where 62% of its answers hit the output cap even when raised from 16K to 32K tokens. As evaluation is costly, each model is run on the full test split in one configuration. We tried various prompts on the validation split and kept the elements with a clear effect on the scores: the camera intrinsics and the in-context examples, which improve format following for some models (Supp. Sec. A.4). Further settings can be evaluated through the online evaluation system. Prompts, decoding parameters, and per-model details are in Supp. Sec. I.

Other methods.

Beyond end-to-end VLMs, we evaluate four additional 3D grounding methods, most in several variants. First, WildDet3D [56] is a promptable monocular 3D detector that can accept a text or 2D box/point prompt, and optionally a depth map. We evaluate it with its own SAM 3-based 2D detection [14] or ground-truth 2D boxes, and with no depth map, the sensor depth map, or one predicted by Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [65] or UniDepthV2 [81]. Second, Boxer [29] lifts a 2D bounding box to a 3D box, using the whole image and, optionally, 3D scene points. We evaluate it in the same settings as WildDet3D, with the gravity direction of each image estimated by GeoCalib [90] (Supp. Sec. J.2). Third, SAM 3D [19] reconstructs the 3D shape, pose, and texture of an object from an image and a 2D mask. It outputs no 3D box, so we take the axis-aligned box of the reconstructed mesh in its canonical frame, placed into the camera by the predicted pose and scale (Supp. Sec. J.3). Fourth, mask back-projection lifts the SAM 3 mask [14] of each Gemini 4 Carbon 2D box with Depth Pro 2 (DP2) depth [55] and fits a box (Supp. Sec. J.4). Like the VLMs, each variant is run 3 times (mask back-projection once).

4.2 Results

3D grounding results (Tab. 2 and Supp. Tab. 6).

Monocular 3D grounding is far from solved. The best VLM, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches only 12.4% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} and the next best, Claude Opus 5.5, 5.3% (Supp. Tab. 6), while the dedicated 3D pipelines WildDet3D and Boxer (run with SAM 3-based detection and Depth Anything 3 depth) score 1.6% and 1.0%. Mask back-projection (Carbon2D + SAM 3 + DP2), which lifts Carbon’s 2D boxes with predicted depth, reaches 7.3%, second only to Carbon’s own 3D boxes. At such low scores, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} says little about how close the predictions come, as a complete miss and a box off by a few centimeters both score zero. APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} (Tab. 2) separates them: it spreads the VLMs from 13.9% to 60.3%, the 12 VLMs below 2% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} alone from 13.9% to 32.5%, and ranks them consistently with APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} (Spearman’s ρ=0.96\rho=0.96).

APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} also shows clear progress across generations, from 18.4% for Claude Opus 4.6 to 46.5% for Opus 5.5, from 24.6% for Gemini 3.1 Pro to 60.3% for Gemini 4 Carbon, and from 24.5% for GPT-5.4 to 39.4% for GPT-6 Astra. Yet precise 3D boxes remain out of reach: even for Gemini 4 Carbon, AP at NCD≤1\text{NCD}\leq 1 (a mean corner error of at most one box diagonal) is only 69.5%. The best open-weight model reaches 26.1% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, less than half of the best proprietary score, whereas in 2D the best open-weight model reaches about 78% of the best proprietary score (Tab. 3).

Across datasets, the industrial IPD and ITODD, with small textureless parts in cluttered scenes, are the hardest for most models (no VLM exceeds 0.3% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} on IPD), and YCB-V, LM, and HB are among the easiest. Gemini 4 Carbon gains most on ITODD (71.1% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} vs. 21.1% for Claude Opus 5.5): the camera distance barely varies there, possibly known from public ITODD data, and Carbon estimates it far more precisely (median error 2% vs. 21%). Over the other eight datasets, Carbon’s mean APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} is 58.9% vs. 49.7%. Per-threshold AP, including APIoU3D​@0.15\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}\text{@0.15} used in recent VLM evaluations [7], is in Supp. Tabs. 9 and 10.

2D grounding results (Tab. 3).

2D grounding is in much better shape. Gemini 4 Carbon leads with 72.6% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}, ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (69.1%) and Claude Opus 5.5 (69.0%), 0.1 points apart and within the run-to-run standard deviation (at most 0.60.6 points). The contrast with 3D is stark even at lenient thresholds: Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 91.1% APIoU2D​@0.50\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}\text{@0.50} but only 17.6% APIoU3D​@0.05\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}\text{@0.05} (Supp. Tabs. 11 and 10). For Claude and GPT, the generational gains are even larger in 2D: APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} grows from 1.3% for Claude Opus 4.6 to 18.8% for Opus 4.7 and 69.0% for Opus 5.5, and from 4.6% for GPT-5.4 to 25.2% for GPT-5.5 and 65.5% for GPT-6 Astra. This suggests that 2D grounding received little attention in earlier models but is a clear focus of recent releases. Among the open-weight models, which otherwise reach 44–57%, Qwen3.5 stands out with 3.8%. Its boxes are shifted by about 4% of the image width to the right on every dataset, unlike those of Qwen3-VL and Qwen3.6 with the same prompt and parser, and we found no cause in our pipeline. Removing it raises its APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} only to 8.6%, so its low score is mostly genuine. As in 3D, IPD is the hardest dataset: Gemini 4 Carbon reaches 68.5% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} on it, but only 11 of the 17 models exceed 25% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}.

4.3 Ablations

VLMs localize the referred objects far better in 2D than in 3D: Gemini 4 Carbon reaches 72.6% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} but only 12.4% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} on the same images and queries (Tab. 3 and Supp. Tab. 6). To find where 3D grounding fails, we ran a range of ablations. Those on query cardinality, target visibility and size, camera intrinsics, few-shot prompting, and output representation are in Supp. Sec. A, and the three that stood out are reported here. Supp. Tab. 4 lists the VLM ablations, and Supp. Tabs. 7 and 8 the specialist pipelines given ground-truth 2D boxes. Each gives the method one piece of ground-truth information that it otherwise has to estimate: the distances between the camera center and the centers of the target objects, the targets’ 2D boxes, or a depth map of the scene. Each ablation is run on the methods that natively accept its input. The distance and 2D-box ablations are run on three strong VLMs, one per lab (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), the 2D-box ablation also on WildDet3D, Boxer, and SAM 3D, and the depth ablation on WildDet3D and Boxer.

Given object distance.

We add each target’s distance from the camera center to the query. APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} grows from 60.3% to 87.5% for Gemini 4 Carbon, from 46.5% to 87.5% for Claude Opus 5.5, and from 39.4% to 90.6% for GPT-6 Astra. AP at NCD≤1\text{NCD}\leq 1 is 96% or more, so nearly all boxes land within one box diagonal of the target, and APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} increases to 58.7%, 49.5%, and 60.1% (from 12.4%, 5.3%, and 3.0%).

Given 2D box.

We add the ground-truth 2D box of each target to the prompt, so only the 3D estimation step is left. The effect is small: APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} changes from 60.3%, 46.5%, and 39.4% to 63.4%, 48.6%, and 43.1%. WildDet3D, Boxer, and SAM 3D take a 2D box as input anyway, from SAM 3 or the ground truth (Supp. Tab. 7). Ground-truth boxes help Boxer most, from 11.5% to 28.1% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, partly because SAM 3 finds nothing for 656 of the 1,400 queries (Supp. Sec. J.5), whereas WildDet3D gains 1.5 pp (6.2 pp with DA3 depth) and SAM 3D 0.5 pp. With ground-truth boxes but no sensor depth, their APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} stays below 5%.

Given depth map.

WildDet3D and Boxer accept depth maps natively. Unlike the distance ablation, which gives a VLM one number per target, a depth map gives the distance of every pixel, from a sensor or a monocular depth estimator. With ground-truth 2D boxes and on the six datasets that provide sensor depth, predicted depth helps moderately and sensor depth much more. WildDet3D improves from 11.6% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} without depth to 19.7% with DA3 and 18.7% with UniDepthV2, and to 33.2% with sensor depth. Boxer improves from 22.4% to 30.0% and 30.8% with predicted depth, and to 79.6% with sensor depth, the only setting that also reaches a high APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} (42.8%, vs. at most 4.1% otherwise).

4.4 Discussion

Why does 3D grounding fail?

The models usually find the referred objects but often misjudge their metric scale. For Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra, we pair each ground-truth box with the predicted box whose center is closest in the image (single-target test queries, Supp. Sec. A.3). The predicted centers lie in almost exactly the right direction from the camera (median error at most 0.6∘), but the boxes have median errors of 7 to 18% in distance and 7 to 15% in size, errors coupled by the size-distance ambiguity of a single view. Such errors are costly in 3D: for the median object, an 8 cm cube at 78 cm, even a correctly sized and oriented box needs a distance error below 6.3% to reach IoU3D≥0.25\text{IoU3D}\geq 0.25, which holds for only 20% (GPT-6 Astra) to 45% (Gemini 4 Carbon) of the predictions. Over all queries, their 2D boxes miss only 1 to 2% of the targets, but their 3D boxes miss 35 to 62%. This is why the ground-truth distance or a depth map helps far more than the ground-truth 2D box (Sec. 4.3). Even given the distance, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} stays at 50 to 60%, so size and orientation are hard to estimate too.

Is 3D grounding solvable?

The low APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} scores raise the question of whether precise monocular 3D grounding is tractable. Existing benchmarks suggest that it is for methods trained for the test setting: specialized models trained on the driving scenes of Mono3DRefer [99] and models trained on Omni3D [12], including Qwen3-VL, reach high accuracy on these benchmarks (Supp. Sec. K). None of the models evaluated in this paper was trained for BOP-Refer, whose objects, sizes, distances, and viewpoints differ from those benchmarks, and all of the models score low. We therefore expect the scores to improve in two ways: with training data closer to the BOP-Refer setting, and with VLMs that learn stronger general priors on object size.

5 Conclusion

We presented BOP-Refer, a benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D object grounding. Built on 9 diverse BOP datasets, the benchmark pairs VLM-generated, human-verified referring expressions with accurate ground-truth boxes derived from 3D object models in annotated 6DoF poses. Our evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs shows that monocular 3D grounding remains a major open challenge, whereas the strongest models already localize most referred objects well in 2D. Most 3D failures thus come not from finding the referred objects but from estimating their metric distance and size, and giving the models the targets’ distances brings by far the largest gains. As a single view constrains only the ratio of size to distance, an important direction for future work is to equip VLMs with stronger priors on the physical size of objects and the ability to infer it from context, e.g., from nearby objects of known size [64]. Our query-generation pipeline applies to any images with 3D object annotations, so it can also produce matching training data, e.g., from the BOP training images, and extend BOP-Refer beyond the BOP objects in future editions. The 3D object models could also enable text-to-shape tasks. We hope BOP-Refer will help drive progress on 3D reasoning in VLMs.
