Supplementary Material

Appendix A Ablation studies

Tab. 4 reports 3D grounding ablations of Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra on the test split. Its first three groups score the default predictions on test-query subsets (Secs. A.1 and A.2). Each subset score averages the datasets with at least one query in the subset (Sec. H), so the default score need not lie between the subset scores. The last two groups change the 3D prompt (Sec. A.4) or add a ground-truth input (Sec. 4.3).

A.1 Single-target vs. multi-target queries

Of the 1,400 test queries, 1,153 refer to a single object and 247 to several. In 2D, cardinality matters little for Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.7 and 0.5 pp APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}), while GPT-6 Astra is better on multi-target queries (69.7% vs. 65.3%). In 3D, single-target queries are easier for all models: APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} is 61.9% vs. 55.2% for Carbon, 47.6% vs. 43.4% for Claude Opus 5.5, and 40.2% vs. 37.2% for GPT-6 Astra. The APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} differences are small for Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra (at most 0.6 pp) and 2.4 pp for Carbon.

A.2 Object visibility and size

We bin each query by the visibility of its least visible target (the visible fraction of the projected object surface: heavily occluded <50%<\!50\%, partially occluded [50,75)%[50,75)\%, mostly visible ≥75%\geq\!75\%) and by the size of its largest target (the 2D-box area as a fraction of the image area: small <1%<\!1\%, medium 11–5%5\%, large >5%>\!5\%). The visibility bins hold 50, 195, and 1,155 test queries, and the size bins 214, 829, and 357. In 2D, all three models score highest on mostly visible targets, and most of the gain comes between partially occluded and mostly visible ones (21.021.0, 20.820.8, and 13.713.7 pp APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}). In 3D, visibility has no consistent effect: APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} varies by at most 2.32.3 pp across the bins for each model, and the APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} of Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 is even slightly higher on heavily occluded targets (14.2% and 8.7%) than on mostly visible ones (12.8% and 5.6%), although with a large run-to-run spread on these 50 queries. The 3D box error thus dominates the cost of occlusion.

Size has the strongest effect. From small to large targets, APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} rises from 49.4% to 73.6% for Gemini 4 Carbon, from 31.1% to 61.2% for Claude Opus 5.5, and from 25.8% to 54.0% for GPT-6 Astra, while APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} rises by only 10.910.9, 9.29.2, and 11.811.8 pp. Small targets also give the lowest APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} of all bins (6.8%, 2.3%, and 1.5%). Part of this effect likely comes from the metrics: NCD and IoU3D are both relative to the object size, so the same absolute position error costs more on a small object than on a large one.

A.3 Error analysis of the 3D predictions

This analysis separates finding the referred object from estimating its metric 3D box (Sec. 4.4). It uses the single-target queries of the test split and the three ablated VLMs (Sec. 4.3), with 3 runs per model (3,247 to 3,458 predictions each). The ground-truth box of each query is matched with the predicted box whose center is closest to the ground-truth center in the image. The two boxes are then compared in the camera frame by the angle between the directions from the camera center to their centers, the ratio of the distances of their centers from the camera center, and the ratio of their sizes (the geometric mean of the three extents). The error of a prediction is the relative error |ρ−1||\rho-1|, where ρ\rho is the ratio of the predicted to the true value. Tab. 5 lists the results.

Required distance accuracy.

Consider a ground-truth cube of side ss and a predicted box with the correct size and orientation whose center is shifted by D≤0.8​sD\leq 0.8\,s. IoU3D is then highest when the shift is along a box axis, where it equals (s−D)/(s+D)(s-D)/(s+D), so IoU3D≥0.25\text{IoU3D}\geq 0.25 requires D≤0.6​sD\leq 0.6\,s and IoU3D≥0.5\text{IoU3D}\geq 0.5 requires D≤s/3D\leq s/3. Because the direction errors are small, the shift lies mostly along the viewing ray, and DD is close to the error of the predicted distance. The median object of the test split has a volume of 528 cm3, that of a cube with a side of 8.1 cm, and the median distance of the objects from the camera is 77.6 cm, so the two thresholds correspond to relative distance errors of 6.3% and 3.5%. Only 20 to 45% and 11 to 29% of the predictions meet them.

Per-dataset bias.

The median distance ratio varies by dataset (bottom of Tab. 5). All models underestimate the distance on IPD (median ratios 0.81 to 0.84) and overestimate it on HOPEv2 (1.07 to 1.35) and HOT3D (1.09 to 1.20).

A.4 Prompt variants

We developed the 3D prompt on the validation split with several VLMs and kept the elements with a clear effect on the scores (Sec. 4.1). Beyond the 9-DoF JSON format of our 3D prompt, which only Qwen and Gemini document as their native 3D box format, we tried other output formats, including Spatial Cookbook–style prompts [36] that place intermediate 2D anchors before the 3D box. None scored noticeably better, so the low scores do not appear to be an artifact of the output representation. The camera intrinsics helped some of the models, and the text-only in-context examples mainly improved format following: for one model, they raised the share of parsable answers from about 75% to 97% and fixed its camera-frame and unit conventions, whereas another parsed about 97% even without them.

The 3D-prompt rows of Tab. 4 measure both elements on the full test split, one at a time. Without the camera intrinsics, APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} changes by −11.7-11.7, −11.1-11.1, and −4.9-4.9 pp (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra). Without in-context examples, it changes by −3.8-3.8, −5.5-5.5, and −1.4-1.4 pp, and Carbon’s share of parsable answers rises from 93.6% to 98.9%, as its longer 5-example prompt more often yields no answer (Sec. I.4), while the others stay at 99.8% and 100.0%. With 10 examples, it changes by −0.4-0.4, +2.0+2.0, and +2.7+2.7 pp. Both elements thus also matter for the strong models, and 5 examples slightly underestimate Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra (by 2.0 and 2.7 pp APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}).

A.5 Run-to-run variability

The VLMs are stochastic, so a single run cannot establish that one model outperforms another. We therefore ran the full evaluation of the test split 3 times for every model, on both tasks, and all result tables report the mean and one standard deviation over these runs. The standard deviation of the overall scores is at most 0.60.6 pp for APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}, well below the gaps between the model groups of Sec. 4.2. For APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, it is at most 1.21.2 pp, well below the 13.813.8 pp lead of Gemini 4 Carbon and the gaps of 6.36.3 and 5.95.9 pp that separate Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon from GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and these from GPT-5.5, but not the gaps of at most 1.01.0 pp within these two pairs. For APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, it is at most 0.70.7 pp. Given the low absolute scores, small differences in APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, such as 2% vs. 1%, are not meaningful even where they exceed the run-to-run standard deviation.

A.6 Query-generator bias

Because the referring expressions are written by VLMs (GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro), a model might be favored by queries its own family generated. The generators produce only text: the ground-truth boxes come from the 3D object models and 6DoF pose annotations, so no information about the answer can leak through a query, and any advantage would have to come from familiarity with the phrasing. We see no sign of such an advantage for the generators themselves. In 3D, GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach only 24.5% and 24.6% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, less than half the score of the best model (60.3%, Gemini 4 Carbon). In 2D, GPT-5.4 reaches only 4.6% APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}, and Gemini 3.1 Pro (61.0%) trails Claude Opus 5.5 (69.0%), whose family generated no queries. Every query was also checked by an independent verifier (Claude Opus 4.7) and by human reviewers, who rewrote or discarded a large share of the candidates, which further dilutes the style of any single generator.

Appendix B Additional result tables

Tab. 6 reports APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} per dataset for the methods of Tab. 2 (Sec. 4.2), and Tabs. 7 and 8 report APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} for the specialist methods given ground-truth 2D boxes (Sec. 4.3). Tabs. 9, 10, and 11 break APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, and APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} down by threshold (Sec. H), and the first two also list the three VLMs of Tab. 4 given the ground-truth object distance or 2D box. Each AP is macro-averaged over the 9 datasets at its threshold, so the overall scores are the row means of these tables, and the single-threshold scores of other works are their columns, e.g., APIoU3D​@0.15\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}\text{@0.15} [7] and APIoU2D​@0.50\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}\text{@0.50} and APIoU2D​@0.75\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}\text{@0.75} [66].

Appendix C Results on the validation split

Tabs. 12, 13, and 14 report APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, and APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} on the validation split for the three ablated VLMs, Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra, evaluated as on the test split. On all three metrics, the three VLMs rank in the same order as on the test split, with overall scores within 2.7 pp of their test scores; the largest differences are those of GPT-6 Astra (+2.7+2.7 pp APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and −2.7-2.7 pp APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}).

Appendix D Qualitative results

Figs. 4–9 (at the end) show validation samples from all 9 source datasets with their queries and ground-truth 3D boxes, together with the 3D boxes predicted by Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra, and Figs. 10–12 show ground-truth and predicted 2D boxes on other samples, one row per dataset. The samples were picked to cover a range of outcomes rather than the typical one. In 3D, they include queries on which all three models succeed, on which only one does, on which all three find the target in the image but miss it in 3D, on which a model boxes a different object or nothing, and multi-target queries. In 2D, they include two per dataset on which all three models are accurate.

The most common 3D failure is the one the projections hide: the predicted box overlaps the target in the image but is off in distance and size, which moves and scales the box along the viewing rays and barely changes its projection. On the test split, the 2D boxes enclosing the projected predicted and ground-truth 3D boxes have an IoU of at least 0.5 for 88%, 83%, and 94% of the queries (first run of Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), yet IoU3D stays below 0.25 for 72 to 89% of them. The NCD and IoU3D values in the figures expose such misses, e.g., for the ITODD query “the top cap”, the projected box of Claude Opus 5.5 nearly coincides with the ground truth, but its NCD is 4.0 and IoU3D 0. Boxing a clearly different object (an IoU of the enclosing 2D boxes below 0.2) is rarer: 2.5%, 2.4%, and 1.6% of the test queries, e.g., GPT-6 Astra for the T-LESS query “the widest of the socket holders on top of the book”. For the HB query “all the objects placed on the blue surface”, Opus 5.5 and Astra box all five targets, but even their closest boxes have IoU3D 0.00 and 0.04.

In 2D, the models localize the referred objects well: the IoU2D between each target and its best-matching box, averaged per query, is at least 0.5 for 96.6%, 96.2%, and 96.6% of the test queries. GPT-6 Astra, however, returns several boxes for 10.2% of the single-target test queries (Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 for 0.9% each), e.g., five boxes for the IPD query “the rightmost T-shaped bracket”.

Appendix E Source datasets and licenses

Tab. 15 summarizes the 9 source BOP datasets. The six everyday-object datasets show household items, toys, and tools, and the three industrial ones mostly textureless or metallic parts. Most targets are hand-sized objects 50 to 100 cm from the camera (Fig. 3).

Frame sampling.

The images are drawn from the BOP test splits and, for HANDAL, HOPEv2, HB, ITODD, and IPD, also from the BOP validation splits. For each dataset, candidates are sampled at equal spacing over the images sorted by scene and image ID (only over the BOP test targets [53] for LM, T-LESS, and YCB-V, and only over images with at least two visible objects for HOT3D and ITODD), which yields at most one image per HOT3D clip. Validation and test images come from disjoint scenes, except for the single ITODD scene and the LM-O scene, which are split by image. The candidates were reduced to the counts of Tab. 15 during query verification. Of all pairs of selected images from the same scene (excluding HOT3D), 91.5% in the test split and 92.0% in the validation split refer to different sets of objects.

Licenses.

BOP-Refer reuses images, 3D object models, and 6DoF pose annotations from 9 publicly released BOP datasets, whose licenses are listed in Tab. 16. We respect each upstream license: BOP-Refer redistributes only the components permitted by the source license, and downstream users inherit the restrictions of each source.

BOP-Refer license.

The new contributions of BOP-Refer (the queries, the derived ground truth, and the toolkit) are released under permissive licenses: the toolkit code under MIT, and the queries and derived annotations under CC BY 4.0, except where derived from a source dataset whose license imposes share-alike or non-commercial restrictions, in which case the upstream license applies to that subset.

Appendix F Ground-truth bounding boxes

3D bounding boxes.

Ground-truth 3D bounding boxes are constructed from the 3D object models and 6DoF pose annotations of the BOP datasets. For each object instance, the ground-truth pose (𝐑P,𝐭P)∈S​E​(3)(\mathbf{R}_{P},\mathbf{t}_{P})\in SE(3) is the rigid transform from the model frame MM to the camera frame CC.

We first fit a canonical oriented bounding box to each 3D model (shared by all its instances), parameterized as (𝐑0,𝐭0,𝐬)(\mathbf{R}_{0},\mathbf{t}_{0},\mathbf{s}), where (𝐑0,𝐭0)(\mathbf{R}_{0},\mathbf{t}_{0}) is the rigid transform from the box frame BB to the model frame MM and 𝐬∈ℝ+3\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{+} are the full extents along the box axes. Then, for each object instance, we compose this canonical box with the ground-truth pose to obtain the 3D bounding box in the camera frame, b3​D=(𝐑,𝐭,𝐬)b_{\mathrm{3D}}=(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{s}), with 𝐑=𝐑P​𝐑0\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{R}_{P}\mathbf{R}_{0} and 𝐭=𝐑P​𝐭0+𝐭P{\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{R}_{P}\mathbf{t}_{0}+\mathbf{t}_{P}}.

Canonical 3D bounding boxes.

For each 3D object model ℳ\mathcal{M}, the canonical 3D bounding box is the tightest oriented 3D box whose axes follow the model’s rotational and reflective symmetries (otherwise the dataset’s up direction, with the remaining axes minimizing the cross-sectional area), so that predictions differing from the ground truth only by a symmetry are scored as equivalent under IoU3D. Its extents 𝐬\mathbf{s} are tightened to the model (code in the BOP-Refer toolkit).

2D bounding boxes.

The 2D ground-truth bounding box of an object instance is the tightest axis-aligned box around the projections π⁡(𝐊,𝐑P​𝐯+𝐭P)\pi(\mathbf{K},\mathbf{R}_{P}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{t}_{P}) of all mesh vertices 𝐯\mathbf{v} of its 3D object model in the ground-truth pose, where π\pi denotes perspective projection with the camera intrinsic matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K}. The box is amodal, covering occluded parts, and truncated at the image borders, as in Omni3D [12].

Appendix G Query generation and verification

This section documents the query generation of Sec. 3.4 and its automatic and manual verification.

G.1 Query generation

Scene graph.

For each selected image we build a scene graph that summarizes everything the ground-truth annotations tell us about the annotated objects: their class, normalized 2D box, distance from the camera, visible fraction, apparent and physical size ranks, a coarse position description, and an explicit list of pairwise spatial relations with qualitative margins. The graph is serialized as YAML and given to the query generator as text alongside the image. Spatial relations are computed from the 6DoF poses rather than being inferred by a model, and the generator is instructed to treat the graph as the sole source of truth for any spatial claim. An abbreviated example follows:

scene_graph: image_size: [1280, 960] num_annotated_objects: 3 bbox_format: [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] normalized to 0-1 relative to image_size note: there may be other visible objects in the scene that are not annotated below objects: - obj_id: 1 class: "ceramic coffee mug" bbox_norm: [0.1406, 0.2917, 0.3281, 0.6042] depth_m: 0.45 visibility: 0.92 apparent_size_rank: 2 physical_size_rank: 3 position_description: "left side" relations: - [left-of, 2, large_margin] - [in-front-of, 2, large_margin] - [left-of, 3, large_margin] - [in-front-of, 3, large_margin] - [nearest-to, 2] - [farthest-from, 3] - obj_id: 2 ...

Object appearance descriptions.

The scene graph carries geometry but no surface detail, and a single image often hides the distinguishing features of an object. We therefore describe every 3D object model once, in advance, independently of any image: each model is rendered from 8 canonical viewpoints distributed around it, and the same two VLMs used for query generation (GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro) are asked for a short name and a 3 to 4 sentence description of its identity, colors and appearance, shape, and typical use. The generators receive these descriptions alongside the scene graph. The prompt, without its example answer, is:

You are looking at 8 rendered views of a single 3D object from a robotics / household dataset. Please provide the following as a JSON object (no markdown, just raw JSON): { "name": "<concise object name, 2-5 words>", "description": "<3-4 sentence description covering what the object is, its color(s) and visual appearance, its overall geometric shape, and what it is typically used for. Be specific and factual based on what you see.>" } If the object appears gray or untextured, describe the geometry and likely identity based on shape alone. If unsure, give your best guess.

Query generation prompt.

The generator receives the image, the camera intrinsics, the scene graph, and the object descriptions, and is asked for 5 candidate queries spanning different referring strategies. It is told explicitly that the evaluated model will see only the image, the intrinsics, and the query. Abbreviated template:

You are generating text queries for a vision benchmark that evaluates language-grounded object localization. Each query will be paired with the attached image and camera intrinsics. An evaluated model will receive ONLY the image, intrinsics, and your query -- not the scene graph or object descriptions below. [Task] Select one or more annotated objects and generate exactly 5 text queries, varying the strategy: - APPEARANCE: color, shape, texture, material - SPATIAL-RELATIONAL: position relative to other objects (must be grounded in scene graph) - COMPARATIVE: distinguish from similar objects - FUNCTIONAL: refer by likely use or category - MULTI-OBJECT: shared property across multiple targets [Key rules] - Exactly one correct grounding per query - Natural language (not commands) - For harder queries, do NOT name the target directly - Minimal but sufficient -- fewest attributes to disambiguate - No pixel coordinates or object IDs; at most 30 words - Spatial claims must correspond to explicit scene graph entries - Prefer queries testing 3D understanding (depth, occlusion, size) [Difficulty scoring] 1-100 scale anchored at: 1-20 (trivial), 21-40 (simple attribute/relation), 41-60 (combined reasoning), 61-80 (fine-grained 3D), 81-100 (multi-step, near-ambiguity resolution) [Output] JSON array of 5 entries, each with: target_object_ids, query, strategy, difficulty, reasoning.

G.2 Automatic verification

Every candidate query is passed to Claude Opus 4.7, a model that took no part in query generation, together with the image, the scene graph, the object descriptions, the intended target objects, and the generator’s strategy, difficulty, and reasoning. The verifier judges the query against the 14 numbered criteria of the prompt below and rejects it if any criterion fails. Of the 21,190 candidate queries generated for the test split, 62.3% passed. Among the 7,984 rejections, the two most often cited criteria are unambiguity (27.7%), where the expression matches several objects, and spatial-anchor quality (25.2%), where the query anchors the target to a landmark that is itself ambiguous, distant, or hallucinated. Abbreviated prompt:

You are a strict quality-assurance reviewer for a VLM benchmark. You receive: an image, the scene graph (all annotated objects with spatial relations), per-object descriptions, and for each query: the text, target IDs, strategy, difficulty, and generator’s reasoning. [Verification criteria -- ALL must pass for "Correct"] 1. Target match: query refers to exactly the listed targets 2. Unambiguity: no other visible object could plausibly match 3. Factual accuracy: all mentioned attributes correct in image 4. Spatial accuracy: spatial claims must appear in target’s scene graph relations list (scene graph is sole source of truth) 5. Reasoning validity: generator’s reasoning must not make false claims 6. Naturalness: reads like natural spoken language 7. No over-description: fewest attributes necessary 8. Difficulty-appropriate indirection: no direct naming for difficulty > 50 9-12. No coordinates, no object counts in multi-target, no stacked comparatives, at most 30 words 13. Strict duplicate-class disambiguation check 14. Spatial queries must use natural, unambiguous, nearby anchors [Output] JSON array: [{"index", "label": "Correct"|"Incorrect", "reason": "..."}, ...]

Tab. 17 breaks the pass rate down by target size and by source dataset. Small targets pass only slightly less often than large ones, so the filter does not disproportionately remove small objects, and every dataset remains well represented, with the industrial datasets of small textureless parts in dense clutter at the low end. At the object level, the same 217 objects appear both in passed and in failed queries, so verification excludes no object systematically.

G.3 Manual verification

The surviving candidates were inspected by 25 human reviewers in a web tool that shows each candidate under its image, with the targets highlighted by red boxes, and lets the reviewer accept the query, rewrite it, or flag the sample as unusable. Reviewers saw 3,347 test samples, where a sample is one image with its candidate queries. For 2,714 samples (81%), the reviewers accepted at least one query as generated, and for 356 (11%), they rewrote a query and kept the rewrite. The remaining 277 samples (8%) were flagged unusable and dropped. A sample was flagged unusable only when no rewrite could produce a sound query, typically because the target is almost fully occluded, only a few pixels across, or too dark or blurred to identify.

A diversity-trimming step then capped each query specification at 1.3×1.3\times the mean occurrence, removing 242 over-represented queries. After the IPD images were reduced to 50, 2,730 verified queries over 1,400 unique images remained. One query per image was then chosen, balancing object coverage and including multi-target queries, which gives the final 1,400 test queries with 1,803 ground-truth boxes in total. The final selection covers the objects of each dataset nearly uniformly (the normalized entropy of the number of queries per object is 0.88 to 0.99 in every dataset of both splits) and spreads the images evenly over the scenes, except in LM and HOPEv2, where one scene contributes a larger share of the images. The validation split went through the same generation, verification, and selection.

Appendix H Evaluation metric details

All three scores, APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}}, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, and APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}}, share the protocol below and differ only in the box comparison function that defines matches, and in the thresholds at which it is applied: APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} uses the symmetry-aware NCD of Eq. (1) with δ∈{0.2,0.4,…,2.0}\delta\in\{0.2,0.4,\ldots,2.0\}, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} uses the symmetry-aware IoU3D of Eq. (2) with τ∈{0.05,0.10,…,0.50}\tau\in\{0.05,0.10,\ldots,0.50\}, and APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} uses IoU2D of axis-aligned rectangles with τ∈{0.50,0.55,…,0.95}\tau\in\{0.50,0.55,\ldots,0.95\} following COCO [66]. NCD is a distance, so a larger threshold is looser, whereas IoU3D and IoU2D are similarities, so a larger threshold is stricter.

H.1 AP protocol

Per-dataset, per-threshold AP.

Write ee for the comparison function of the score being computed and Θ\Theta for its set of thresholds (ten for each of the three scores). For each dataset DD and each θ\theta, APD,θ\text{AP}_{D,\theta} is computed as follows:

  1. 1.

    For each query q∈Dq\in D, the model’s predictions are sorted by descending confidence and truncated to the top 100.

  2. 2.

    Predictions are greedily assigned, in confidence order, to the still-unmatched ground-truth box that ee ranks best among those already passing the threshold test, i.e., the smallest NCD≤θ\text{NCD}\leq\theta for APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and the highest IoU3D≥θ\text{IoU3D}\geq\theta or IoU2D≥θ\text{IoU2D}\geq\theta for the overlap scores. Each ground-truth box is matched to at most one prediction, and the assignment is recomputed independently for every θ\theta, following COCO [66]. Assigned predictions are true positives, and unassigned ones false positives.

  3. 3.

    All labeled predictions from DD are pooled and ranked by descending confidence, yielding one precision–recall curve. Predictions with equal confidence form a single operating point: within a tie, false positives are ranked before true positives, so every recall level inside the tie gets the precision of the whole tie, and the precision–recall curve does not depend on how tied predictions are ranked (within a query, ties are matched in file order). For the VLMs, whose confidences come from the box order in each answer (Supp. Sec. I.4), all first boxes form one operating point, all second boxes the next, and so on.

  4. 4.

    The (monotonically enveloped) precision is averaged over 101 equally-spaced recall points r∈{0,0.01,…,1.0}r\in\{0,0.01,\ldots,1.0\} to obtain APD,θ\text{AP}_{D,\theta}.

Aggregation.

The per-dataset score is the mean over its thresholds, APD=1|Θ|​∑θ∈ΘAPD,θ\text{AP}_{D}=\tfrac{1}{|\Theta|}\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}\text{AP}_{D,\theta}, and the headline score is the mean across the 9 datasets, AP=19​∑DAPD\text{AP}=\tfrac{1}{9}\sum_{D}\text{AP}_{D}. Queries on LM-O images count under LM (Tab. 15).

Subset metrics.

For breakdowns by query or target category (e.g., single- vs. multi-target queries, visibility or size bins), the same protocol is applied to the subset of queries, and the headline subset score is the mean across datasets that have at least one query in the subset.

H.2 Symmetry-aware Normalized Corner Distance

Corner labelings.

A box b=(𝐑,𝐭,𝐬)b=(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{s}) with rotation 𝐑\mathbf{R}, center 𝐭\mathbf{t}, and extents 𝐬\mathbf{s} has the corners 𝐜𝝈​(b)=𝐑⁡(𝝈⊙𝐬)/2+𝐭\mathbf{c}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(b)=\mathbf{R}\,(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\odot\mathbf{s})/2+\mathbf{t}, indexed by the sign vectors 𝝈∈{−1,1}3\boldsymbol{\sigma}\in\{-1,1\}^{3}. This parameterization is not unique. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the group of the 24 rotations that map a cube onto itself, i.e., the signed permutation matrices with determinant 11. For every 𝐏∈𝒪\mathbf{P}\in\mathcal{O}, the box (𝐑𝐏,𝐭,|𝐏|⊤​𝐬)(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P},\mathbf{t},|\mathbf{P}|^{\top}\mathbf{s}), whose extents are permuted along with its axes, is the same box with relabeled corners, 𝐜𝝈​(𝐑𝐏,𝐭,|𝐏|⊤​𝐬)=𝐜𝐏​𝝈​(𝐑,𝐭,𝐬)\mathbf{c}_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P},\mathbf{t},|\mathbf{P}|^{\top}\mathbf{s})=\mathbf{c}_{\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma}}(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{s}), where |𝐏||\mathbf{P}| takes absolute values elementwise. The corner permutations in Eq. (1) are therefore Π={𝝈↦𝐏​𝝈:𝐏∈𝒪}\Pi=\{\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mapsto\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma}:\mathbf{P}\in\mathcal{O}\}.

These 24 relabelings include the self-symmetries of the box, i.e., the 𝐏\mathbf{P} that leave its extents in place (4 for three distinct extents, 8 for a square prism, 24 for a cube), and those that interchange distinct extents, which occur when a method orders the box axes differently from the ground truth. All 24 describe the same box, so the minimum over Π\Pi needs no extent tolerance and never credits a different box.

What NCD=0\text{NCD}=0 certifies.

Since every relabeling maps the corner set of a box onto itself, a prediction that describes the ground-truth box in a different parameterization yields NCD=0\text{NCD}=0, whereas a fixed corner correspondence would penalize it, e.g., by 0.820.82 for a cube turned by 180∘180^{\circ} about an axis. Conversely, NCD=0\text{NCD}=0 implies that the predicted box coincides with 𝐒∘b3​D\mathbf{S}\circ b_{\mathrm{3D}} for some 𝐒∈𝒮\mathbf{S}\in\mathcal{S}, and thus IoU3D=1\text{IoU3D}=1.

Orientation-only errors.

Normalizing by the ground-truth box diagonal bounds orientation-only errors by a shape-independent constant: a prediction with the correct center and extents that differs from the ground truth only by a rotation has NCD≤1/2≈0.71\text{NCD}\leq 1/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.71. Over the four relabelings in 𝒪\mathcal{O} that keep the extents in place, every coordinate of a corner is negated by exactly two, so the squared distance of each corner averages to d​(b3​D)2/2d(b_{\mathrm{3D}})^{2}/2, and the best relabeling has a root-mean-square, and hence mean, corner distance of at most d⁡(b3​D)/2d(b_{\mathrm{3D}})/\sqrt{2}. An NCD above 1/21/\sqrt{2} therefore implies an error in translation or extents.

Relation to prior corner-distance metrics.

Distance-based localization metrics have precedent in nuScenes [13], which thresholds the center distance on the ground plane instead of IoU3D but, as Brazil et al. [12] note, thereby ignores object size and rotation, whereas NCD is sensitive to all three. Corner-distance metrics for 3D boxes have also been proposed, most closely the Normalized Hungarian Distance (NHD) [10], which, like our NCD, measures corner-to-corner error normalized by the ground-truth box diagonal (we average NHD over the 8 corners, like NCD). The two metrics resolve the corner-labeling ambiguity differently. NHD re-matches the 8 predicted and ground-truth corners by optimal assignment (the Hungarian algorithm) and thus admits all 8!=40,3208!=40{,}320 corner permutations, whereas NCD admits only the 24 in Π\Pi, which correspond to rigid relabelings of the box. Without object symmetries, NHD therefore never exceeds NCD, but the two are close in practice: over 4,0004{,}000 random poses of each of four box shapes, they coincide in 32%32\% to 63%63\% of the cases, with a median difference below 0.0010.001 and a maximum of 0.120.12.

The substantive difference is that NCD also minimizes over the object symmetries 𝒮\mathcal{S}, as IoU3D does, whereas NHD compares the boxes regardless of the object. For a cylinder whose 1×1×31\times 1\times 3 box is turned by 45∘45^{\circ} about the cylinder axis (Fig. 2d), NHD is 0.160.16 although the turned box is an equally valid ground truth, whereas NCD is 00 and IoU3D is 11. NCD is also related to pose errors that measure distances between object model points instead of box corners, such as ADD(-S) [49, 92] and the MSSD of the BOP challenges [53], which handle symmetries in the same way (see Hodaň et al. [50] for a discussion of ambiguity-invariant pose errors).

Appendix I VLM prompts

This section lists the prompts used to evaluate the VLMs, the output parsing, and the decoding parameters. All models receive the same 3D prompt, our own, which asks for 9-DoF boxes, whereas each model family receives its own zero-shot 2D prompt in its documented box convention. Line breaks within paragraphs were added for readability.

I.1 3D grounding prompt

All models receive the 3D prompt below, with 5 text-only in-context examples (Sec. I.2). It gives the image size and the camera intrinsics and asks for 9-DoF boxes in the OpenCV camera frame, in meters and degrees.

System: You are an expert 3D spatial reasoning model. User: <image> Image size: {W}x{H} px. Camera intrinsics [fx, fy, cx, cy]: [{fx}, {fy}, {cx}, {cy}]. Given the provided image and camera intrinsics, predict 3D bounding boxes of the following objects: "{query}". Output conventions: (1) Report the 3D bounding boxes in the OpenCV camera frame (X right, Y down, Z forward) as a JSON list: [{"box_3d": [x_center, y_center, z_center, x_size, y_size, z_size, roll, pitch, yaw], "label": "{query}"}, ...]. (2) Center and size are in meters; roll/pitch/yaw are in degrees. (3) x, y, z: 3D box center in the camera coordinate frame, in meters. (4) Camera frame follows OpenCV convention (+x right, +y down, +z forward from the camera). (5) w, h, d: full box extents in meters along the object’s own axes. (6) roll, pitch, yaw: rotation in degrees (extrinsic Tait-Bryan XYZ). The rotation maps the object’s canonical axes into the camera frame (OpenCV). (7) If no object matches the query, return [].

I.2 Few-shot in-context examples (3D task)

In the 3D prompt, the system message is followed by 5 alternating (user, assistant) turn pairs and then by a final user turn with the test query. Each example user turn is the same user turn filled in for another query, without an image, and each assistant turn is the ground-truth list of 9-DoF boxes of that query, in meters and degrees, under the key box_3d. The examples therefore convey only the expected output schema and the camera-frame and unit conventions, not visual information. The examples are 5 queries from the validation split. Gemini Robotics ER 2 receives them as text in the single user turn instead of as separate turns. Without the examples, APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} of the three ablated VLMs (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra) drops by 1.4 to 5.5 pp, and with 10 examples it changes by −0.4-0.4 to +2.7+2.7 pp relative to 5 examples (Sec. A.4).

I.3 2D grounding prompts

Each model family receives its own system and user prompt, listed verbatim below. The user turn contains the image followed by the text, without camera intrinsics. Except for the GPT family, for which we found no documented box format and request absolute pixel coordinates, the prompts ask for boxes in each family’s documented coordinate convention. Only the prompts for GPT and Claude ask for amodal boxes.

Gemini.

Used by Gemini 3.1 Pro, 3.8 Flash, 4 Argon, and 4 Carbon. Boxes as [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized to [0,1000][0,1000]. The user prompt follows the object-detection example of Google’s Gemini spatial-understanding notebook, including its label instruction:

System: You are Gemini’s visual grounding system. Output bounding boxes in your native [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] format, normalized to 0-1000. User: <image> Detect the 2d bounding boxes of the {query} (with "label" as topping description").

Gemini Robotics ER 2.

Same box format as Gemini, with the system message prepended to the user text:

System: You are Gemini Robotics ER, a helpful visual grounding assistant. User: <image> Return bounding boxes as a JSON array with labels highlighting {query}. The format should be as follows: [{"box_2d": [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax], "label": }] normalized to 0-1000. The values in box_2d must only be integers.

Gemma 4.

Same box format as Gemini:

System: You are Gemma’s visual grounding system. Output bounding boxes in your native [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] format, normalized to 0-1000. User: <image> Detect {query}. Output only ```json".

GPT.

Used by GPT-5.4, 5.5, 6 Astra, and 6.1 Sol. Boxes as [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] in pixels:

System: You are GPT, a helpful visual grounding assistant. User: <image> Return a tight AMODAL 2D bounding box for every distinct object instance that matches {query}. AMODAL means the box must cover the whole object, including any occluded parts. Output bounding boxes in image pixel coordinates. Output format should be a JSON list with each entry of the format: {"label": "<short name>", "bbox_2d": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max]}. If nothing matches, return [].

Claude.

Used by Claude Opus 4.6, 4.7, and 5.5. Boxes as [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] in absolute pixel coordinates, with the image resolution stated in the user turn:

System: You are Claude, an expert visual grounding assistant. Output bounding boxes in your native [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] format, in pixel coordinates. User: <image> Image resolution: {W} x {H} pixels (width x height). Referring expression: "{query}". Find EVERY distinct object instance in the image that matches the referring expression. For each match, return a tight AMODAL 2D bounding box enclosing the WHOLE object (including any parts that are occluded in this view). Output a single JSON list with each entry as: {"label": "<short name>", "bbox_2d": [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max]}. If nothing matches, return [].

Qwen.

Used by Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6, and Qwen3.8 Flash Next. Boxes as [x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max] normalized to [0,1000][0,1000], matching Qwen’s public grounding format:

System: You are Qwen, a helpful visual grounding assistant. User: <image> locate every instance that belongs to the following categories: {query}. Report bbox coordinates, in JSON format.

Because Claude is prompted in its documented box convention, and the boxes of Claude Opus 4.6 are mapped back from the API-downscaled image frame (Sec. I.4), the low 2D score of Claude Opus 4.6 in Tab. 3 is a genuine measurement rather than an artifact of a foreign output convention.

I.4 Output parsing

All responses go through a shared parser. It keeps the text after the last “Final Answer:” tag if there is one, strips markdown code fences, and parses the rest as JSON, falling back to the first balanced JSON array or object if that fails. Predictions that still fail to parse count as zero detections. For Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini Robotics ER 2, calls that return no answer, typically because thinking used up the token budget, are re-sampled up to 5 times (ER 2 also when cut off). This yields an answer for about 22% of Carbon’s 3D test queries, and the roughly 6% still without one after 5 re-samples count as misses, so its 3D scores are slightly underestimated. ER 2 needed this for at most one query per run, and the other models, which are not re-sampled, rarely return empty answers (GPT-5.5: about 5%).

2D boxes.

They are converted to pixels from the convention each model is prompted in (Sec. I.3). Boxes requested in absolute pixel coordinates (Claude and GPT models) are rescaled only when all their coordinates are at most 1.5, i.e., normalized to [0,1][0,1]. Boxes are clipped to the image. The Claude API downscales images to roughly 1.15 megapixels and at most 1,568 pixels on the long side before Opus 4.6 sees them, and it returns its 2D boxes in the downscaled frame, so we map them back to the original image. Claude Opus 4.7 and 5.5 return boxes in the original frame.

3D boxes.

The parser accepts the box_3d, bbox_3d, box, and bbox keys, also nested under keys such as objects, flattens boxes given as three nested triples, sets missing angles to zero, and reads six-value boxes as axis-aligned min/max corners. To catch unit errors, a box whose center coordinates are all below 20 in magnitude is read as meters, and otherwise as millimeters. Angles are read as degrees. Following the official Qwen 3D grounding cookbook [7], the Qwen 3D boxes are read as metric boxes in the camera frame, since applying the Omni3D virtual-camera depth denormalization [12] instead degraded their scores. No other model receives a model-specific adjustment.

Confidences.

None of the prompts asks for a confidence, so we derive one from the order of the boxes in each answer: the ii-th box gets the confidence 1−10−4​(i−1)1-10^{-4}(i-1). A model’s first box thus ranks before its second box, while boxes at the same position in different answers are tied (Supp. Sec. H). Every model lists its most reliable box first: compared with tying all boxes, ranking them by their order raises APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} by 0.3 to 1.5 percentage points for every VLM, APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}} by at most 0.2, and APIoU2D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU2D}} by 0.1 to 2.2, except for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol (+6.6+6.6 and +7.5+7.5), which often add lower-ranked candidate boxes.

I.5 Decoding parameters

The proprietary models run at medium reasoning effort (or thinking level). Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6, and Qwen3.8 Flash Next, served via NVIDIA, are run with thinking on (Qwen3.6 off in 3D: with thinking, 62% of its answers hit the token cap), and Qwen3-VL (thinking off) and Gemma 4 with the OpenRouter defaults. The sampling temperature is 0.60.6 for Gemma 4 and Qwen3-VL in 2D, 11 for GPT-5.5, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 4.6, 4.7, and 5.5, and Gemini Robotics ER 2, and 0.10.1 for the other models. Responses are capped at 4,096 output tokens (8,000 for GPT-6.1 Sol, 16,384 for Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 Flash Next in 3D, 32,768 for Carbon and the other Qwen runs except Qwen3-VL in 2D, 65,536 for ER 2). Unparsable responses are not re-queried.

Appendix J Other 3D grounding methods

This section describes how the other 3D grounding methods in Tabs. 2, 6, 7, and 8 are implemented. They use public checkpoints without fine-tuning (mask back-projection also uses Gemini 4 Carbon) and run on every test image with its camera intrinsics. The rows fall into two groups. In Tabs. 2 and 6, the referred objects are localized from the text query alone: WildDet3D uses its own text-grounded 2D head, which is built on SAM 3 [14], while Boxer and SAM 3D use 2D boxes and masks predicted by SAM 3 (Sec. J.5), and mask back-projection uses the 2D boxes of Gemini 4 Carbon (Sec. J.4). In Tabs. 7 and 8, each method instead receives one prompt per ground-truth 2D box of the query’s target objects, which factors out 2D detection errors. WildDet3D and Boxer without depth are deterministic, whereas the Boxer rows with depth and SAM 3D vary slightly across runs because of the random sampling of points and seeds (Sec. J.2).

J.1 WildDet3D

Model.

WildDet3D [56] is a promptable monocular 3D detector. It takes an RGB image, the intrinsic matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K}, an optional dense depth map, and a text, 2D-box, or 2D-point prompt, and returns a 2D box and a 9-DoF 3D box per detected object in the camera frame. Every image is fitted into a 1008×10081008\times 1008 canvas (the longer side resized to 1008 pixels, the shorter side zero-padded, and the intrinsics and box prompts transformed accordingly), and non-maximum suppression is applied at IoU 0.60.6.

Prompting.

In Tabs. 2 and 6, WildDet3D runs in its native text-prompt mode: the benchmark query is passed as the input text, the internal text-grounded 2D head proposes the objects, and all 3D candidates with a score of at least 0.30.3 (the upstream default) are kept as predictions. The four rows using ground-truth 2D detections run WildDet3D in box-prompt mode. Each ground-truth 2D box is passed as a separate prompt together with the generic text label object, which scored better than the upstream default label geometric: object and the full query. The score threshold is lowered to 00 so that every prompt returns a candidate, and the best candidate of each prompt is kept.

Depth.

The rows differ in the depth map passed to WildDet3D: none (the monocular geometry head is used), depth predicted by Depth Anything 3 (DA3) or UniDepthV2 [81] (Sec. J.5), or the real sensor depth provided with the images. Depth maps are resampled into the canvas with nearest-neighbour interpolation, which avoids blending foreground and background depths at object silhouettes. HOT3D, HANDAL, and IPD provide no dense depth, so the sensor-depth rows of WildDet3D and Boxer are reported as -- on these datasets and without an overall score.

The depth map is passed in meters with depth input enabled, as the WildDet3D README specifies, and WildDet3D does use it: the median ratio of predicted to true object distance falls from 1.21–4.49 per dataset without depth to 1.09–1.89 with sensor depth. It still places objects too far, whereas Boxer, given the same depth maps, is within 3% of the true distance on every dataset. This matches how WildDet3D is trained: 70% of its training samples have no depth input, 20% a patch-masked depth map, and only 10% the full depth map [56, Sec. 2.1].

J.2 Boxer

Model.

Boxer [29] detects objects with an open-vocabulary 2D detector and lifts each 2D detection to an oriented 3D box with a transformer called BoxerNet. We use the official release v1.0.0 (tag ef6cad8) with the public boxernet_hw960in2x6d768-c88128f8.ckpt checkpoint and bypass the built-in 2D detector: BoxerNet receives either every SAM 3 box of the query with a score of at least 0.30.3, the same boxes as SAM 3D (Tabs. 2 and 6, where queries for which SAM 3 returns no such box get no prediction) or each ground-truth 2D box as a separate prompt (Tabs. 7 and 8). The image is resized to 960×960960\times 960 with correspondingly rescaled intrinsics, and the predictions are mapped back to the original image.

Single-image inference.

Boxer is designed for video with known per-frame camera poses and a semi-dense point cloud. Its README also covers single images given the camera intrinsics and the direction of gravity, and lists only images without this information as untested. BoxerNet regresses gravity-aligned boxes, so it needs the direction of gravity in the camera frame. Since many BOP-Refer views are tilted, we estimate the gravity direction of each image with GeoCalib [90], as the Boxer authors suggest for inputs without known gravity, and set the camera pose passed to Boxer accordingly. The rows without depth pass an empty point cloud. In the rows with depth (+ DA3, + UniDepthV2, and + sensor depth), the depth map, the same as for WildDet3D, is back-projected into a 3D point cloud with the camera intrinsics, and 10,000 points sampled from it at random, with a new seed per run, are passed as Boxer’s point input.

J.3 SAM 3D

Model.

SAM 3D [19] is a generative single-image 3D object reconstructor. From an RGB image and a binary object mask, it produces a textured mesh of the object in a canonical frame, with a 6DoF pose and an isotropic scale that place the mesh into the camera. We use the released checkpoints/hf/pipeline.yaml configuration. It uses neither the camera intrinsics nor a depth map, so it infers the distance and scale of the object from the image alone, without any metric reference.

Masks.

In Tabs. 2 and 6, every mask that SAM 3 returns for the query with a score of at least 0.30.3 is lifted to a separate prediction, and queries without such a mask get no prediction. In Tabs. 7 and 8, each ground-truth 2D box is rasterized into a rectangular mask at the original image resolution.

From mesh to 3D box.

SAM 3D outputs no 3D box, so we take the axis-aligned box of the reconstructed mesh in its canonical frame: its extents are the per-axis ranges of the mesh vertices multiplied by the predicted scale, and it is placed into the camera by the predicted pose, converted from the PyTorch3D to the OpenCV camera convention by a 180∘180^{\circ} rotation about the optical axis. Its center is the predicted translation, i.e., the center of SAM 3D’s canonical cube, which need not coincide with the center of the mesh. The canonical frame is gravity-aligned and unrelated to the oriented-box frame that BOP-Refer fits to each object model (Supp. Sec. F), so its axes and center can differ from the ground truth even for a perfect reconstruction. The SAM 3D scores therefore measure this canonical-box approximation rather than the quality of the reconstruction.

Box size.

With ground-truth 2D boxes, the boxes are 2.6 times too large (median ratio of the cube roots of the volumes), mostly because SAM 3D places them 1.9 times too far away, where an object must be larger to cover the same pixels. With each box’s distance error divided out, they are still 1.5 times too large (1.1–1.2 on HB, LM, and HOT3D, and 1.15 for Boxer), so part of the excess likely comes from the reconstructed shape or from our axis-aligned box, which is loose for objects not aligned with the canonical axes.

J.4 Mask back-projection

Pipeline.

This baseline combines VLM grounding, object masks, and monocular metric depth: Gemini 4 Carbon localizes the referred objects in 2D, and the mask of the object in each 2D box is back-projected to 3D with a predicted depth map. The 2D boxes come from one of Carbon’s three default 2D test runs (1,800 boxes for the 1,400 queries), and each box yields one 3D box with the box’s confidence, derived from its position in Carbon’s answer (Sec. I.4). It uses no ground truth at test time and is run once.

Masks and depth.

SAM 3 [14] computes the masks, prompted with each Carbon box rather than with the text query as for Boxer and SAM 3D (Sec. J.5), and the mask is eroded by 3 pixels. SAM 2.1 [87] masks give nearly the same scores (46.0% APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} and 7.3% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, vs. 45.7% and 7.3%). The depth map is predicted at full resolution by the H+ model of Depth Pro 2 [55], given the true focal length. We selected this estimator on the validation split among seven monocular depth estimators, including Depth Anything 3 and UniDepthV2, as the one whose median depth in the object mask is most often within 10% of the depth of the ground-truth box center (45% of the objects, vs. 41% for DA3 and 29% for UniDepthV2).

From points to 3D box.

The masked pixels are back-projected with the true intrinsics, points with a depth outside the 5th to 95th percentile of the mask are dropped, and the 3D box is the bounding box of the remaining points along their principal axes. The points cover only the visible surface of the object, so the box leaves out its occluded parts. Its APNCD\text{AP}_{\text{NCD}} exceeds that of Carbon’s 3D boxes on HOT3D, LM, and IPD but is only 12.5% and 0.0% on T-LESS and ITODD, although its 2D boxes are accurate there (Tab. 3).

J.5 Off-the-shelf input predictors

SAM 3 (2D boxes and masks for Boxer and SAM 3D).

We run SAM 3 [14], a text-promptable open-vocabulary segmenter, on each image with the benchmark query, and cache the returned masks, boxes, and confidence scores, keeping detections with a score of at least 0.30.3, the threshold WildDet3D applies to its own text head. SAM 3 returns such a detection for 744 of the 1,400 test queries, and the other 656 queries count as misses for Boxer and SAM 3D in Tabs. 2 and 6. SAM 3 misses them because it expects short noun phrases rather than full referring expressions.

Depth Anything 3 and UniDepthV2.

For the + DA3 and + UniDepthV2 rows, we use the depth-anything/DA3NESTED-GIANT-LARGE checkpoint of Depth Anything 3 [65] at a processing resolution of 504 pixels and the ViT-L/14 checkpoint lpiccinelli/unidepth-v2-vitl14 of UniDepthV2 [81], both conditioned on the camera intrinsics of each image. Both predict metric depth, which we use directly, without scale or shift alignment, and the DA3 depth map is resized bilinearly to the original image resolution.

Appendix K BOP-Refer vs. Omni3D data distribution

Fig. 3 compares the data distributions of BOP-Refer and Omni3D. The median BOP-Refer object has a volume of 528​cm3528\,\mathrm{cm}^{3} (an 8 cm cube), whereas the median Omni3D object has about 1.9×105​cm31.9\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{cm}^{3} (furniture and vehicles), roughly 350×350\times larger. Likewise, 83.1%83.1\% of the Omni3D test annotations lie more than 200200 cm from the camera but only 0.3%0.3\% of the BOP-Refer ones, which concentrate at arm’s length (median depth 7676 cm). On the image side, Omni3D is dominated by a single focal-length and resolution mode (from Hypersim), whereas BOP-Refer spans the distinct sensors of its nine sources. Its close-up objects come mainly from Objectron [2], which covers nine categories and has no referring expressions. The gap may also explain why VLMs whose 3D training data follows the conventions and source datasets of Omni3D, most notably Qwen3-VL [7], score high on Omni3D yet transfer poorly to BOP-Refer (Sec. 4.2).

Scores of trained models on existing benchmarks.

Models trained for an existing monocular 3D grounding benchmark score high on it. On Mono3DRefer [99], a KITTI-derived benchmark with the same input-output structure as BOP-Refer, Mono3DVG-EnSD [63] reaches 69.5%69.5\% Acc@0.25. On Omni3D, LocateAnything3D [71] reaches 38.9%38.9\% APIoU3D\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}, and Qwen3-VL reaches 39.4%39.4\% mAP@0.15 on SUN-RGBD, which we reproduced. On BOP-Refer, Qwen3-VL reaches 1.9%1.9\% APIoU3D​@0.15\text{AP}_{\text{IoU3D}}\text{@0.15} (Tab. 10).
